title: Victim loses £250k after scammers use AI video of 'well-known' celebrity

reading.body:
This is an impersonation carried out with synthetic media. An AI-generated video appeared to show a well-known figure from the financial sector endorsing an investment, and the victim treated that apparent endorsement as evidence the offer was real. The impersonation did not attack a bank or a trading system, it attacked the step where a person decides whether a counterparty exists and can be trusted.

The fraud then moved off the advert and into direct contact. Scammers reached the victim on WhatsApp, pressed for escalating payments, had the victim open several online accounts, and took remote access to the victim's computer under the claim of helping with the investment. The victim borrowed money to keep paying. Each of those steps is a point where the transaction could have been stopped, and none of them required the criminals to defeat a technical control, only to keep the victim convinced.

Catching it would have meant verifying the identity of the person and the firm independently of the advert, which is what the Police Service of Northern Ireland advised, along with checking Financial Conduct Authority authorisation. What is not established is who the figure in the video was, whether that person had any involvement in or knowledge of the scam, and whether anyone has been charged or convicted. The police account describes a fraud under investigation, not a proven case against a named party.

reports.title: Victim loses £250k after scammers use AI video of 'well-known' celebrity

summary:
A person in the Ards and north Down area of Northern Ireland lost £250,000 in an investment scam. The Police Service of Northern Ireland said the victim saw an AI-generated video that appeared to feature a well-known financial sector figure. The advert promised an investment opportunity and large returns. After a small initial payment, scammers contacted the victim on WhatsApp and pushed for more money. They persuaded the victim to open several online accounts and gave them remote access to the victim's computer, claiming to help with the investment.

Police described it as a complex, large-scale fraud. The criminals built trust and sought increasingly large payments, even getting the victim to borrow money, which went to accounts they controlled. The PSNI did not name the celebrity. Police warned that an apparent celebrity endorsement does not prove an investment is genuine. They advised people to independently verify who they are dealing with and to check Financial Conduct Authority authorisation. Police also urged people to pause and verify and families to talk about fraud.
